Rideshare entry expanded service — shorter waits and far better coverage of outer-borough and historically underserved neighbourhoods that yellow cabs rarely served (Schaller's analyses of NYC trip data)

The medallion price collapse (to roughly $150-200k within a few years) was a real capital loss, and it fell heavily on immigrant owner-drivers who had been sold medallions at inflated prices with predatory loans (NYT 2019 investigation) — the asset bubble was inflated by brokers, lenders and the city selling medallions as investments, not created by Uber alone
Rideshare is not a free lunch: it added vehicle-miles and congestion in dense cores (Schaller 2018), which is a genuine cost that the 'competition good' story must carry
acceptable_nuances: Yellow-cab service also discriminated by destination/race in ways app dispatch reduced — part of the coverage story
Whether drivers earn more under rideshare than under the medallion lease system is mixed and city-dependent
forbidden_claims: Medallion caps had no effect on taxi supply or prices
The medallion crash was caused solely by rideshare companies, with no role for lenders, brokers or the city's own medallion sales
Rideshare entry produced no benefits for passengers outside wealthy downtown cores
sources_note: NYC TLC trip data as analysed in Schaller (2017, 2018) reports on geographic coverage and VMT; NYT (2019) medallion-debt investigation (peak >$1M, insider-inflated prices, predatory loans); Jacobs (2022), Columbia Human Rights Law Review note, for the fall to ~$150k. Medallion count confirmed: NYC TLC (official Yellow Cab page) states by law there are 13,587 taxis/medallions in New York City. Count is not load-bearing.

question: Why did Americans, until 2026, have access to fewer and older sunscreen UV filters than Europeans or Australians?
required_claims: Because the FDA regulates sunscreen actives as over-the-counter drugs rather than cosmetics, and it approved no new OTC sunscreen ingredient between 1999 and June 2026 — while modern filters (bemotrizinol/Tinosorb S, Mexoryl compounds, Tinosorb M) were in routine use in the EU and Australia from around 2000

Bemotrizinol is the type case: authorised in Europe in 1999 and in use from 2000, filed with the FDA in 2005 under the 'time and extent' pathway (21 CFR 330.14; Sunscreen Innovation Act 2014) that was meant to decide within months, not decades, and only added to the US monograph in June 2026 — a two-decade lag for a molecule with a quarter-century of foreign market exposure

The clinical stakes are real but should not be overstated: dermatology literature identifies UVA protection as the main gap in US formulations; there is no rigorous study quantifying a death toll from the lag, and gold does not invent one
This is the FDA's Type-II-error asymmetry (see econ-fda-net-01) in a low-risk consumer product: the cost of delay fell on nobody's desk, so delay was free for the regulator
acceptable_nuances: The FDA's stated reason — wanting more systemic-absorption safety data for a daily-use, whole-body product — is not frivolous on its face; the calibration failure is treating 25 years of foreign use as near-zero evidence

Congress intervened repeatedly (Sunscreen Innovation Act 2014; CARES Act monograph reform 2020; SAFE Sunscreen Standards Act) — the lag was a process failure acknowledged across parties, not a partisan story
forbidden_claims: US and European sunscreens offered equivalent UV protection throughout 2000-2025
The FDA approved new sunscreen filters at a normal pace and the lag is a myth
It is proven that the sunscreen lag caused a specific large number of skin-cancer deaths (no such estimate exists in the literature)
sources_note: Wang & Lim et al., and Sadr & Lu (2014), Nature Biotechnology / 'Protect the USA from UVA', Nature (2014): no new OTC sunscreen ingredient since 1999, eight applications pending, bemotrizinol in TEA queue since 2005, EU-authorised 1999 (in use from 2000); FDA June 2026 bemotrizinol monograph addition (first since the late 1990s) as reported by FDA/Healio and dermatology press. CONCRETE SIBLING of econ-fda-net-01: same mechanism, checkable dates.

question: What does occupational licensing do to workers' pay and to their ability to move between states for work?
required_claims: Licensed workers earn a substantial wage premium — on the order of 10-15% after controls (Kleiner & Krueger 2013) — while licensing spread from roughly 5% of the US workforce in the 1950s to about a quarter or more today, far faster than unionisation (which moved the other way)

Because licences are state-specific, they function as a moving tax: Johnson & Kleiner (2020) find the between-state migration rate for workers in occupations with state-specific licensing exam requirements is 36% lower than for members of other occupations, while occupations with national licensing exams show no evidence of limited interstate migration
The premium-plus-immobility pattern is what a rent story predicts; a pure human-capital story would not predict that the same worker's credential loses value at a state line
acceptable_nuances: The mobility evidence is not unanimous: studies of specific reciprocity compacts (e.g. the Nurse Licensure Compact; DePasquale & Stange) find little or no migration response — suggesting the barrier binds unevenly across occupations
Some of the wage premium reflects genuine training requirements in some occupations; the estimates with rich controls shrink but do not eliminate it
Johnson & Kleiner's own conclusion: the licensing effect, while real for state-specific-exam occupations, explains only a small part of the overall decline in interstate migration
forbidden_claims: Occupational licensing has no measurable effect on interstate migration
The licensing wage premium proves licensing mainly certifies higher quality
sources_note: Kleiner & Krueger (2013), J Labor Econ (premium ~14-15% in Kleiner & Krueger's multivariate estimates; 10-15% range across studies with standard controls; licensed share ~29% in their survey); Johnson & Kleiner (2020), American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 12(3):347–373 (NBER WP 24107): between-state migration 36% lower for workers in occupations with state-specific licensing exam requirements, relative to other occupations; no evidence of limited migration for occupations with national exams (+5.5% point estimate); all licensed occupations combined −22.5%, and state-specific vs quasi-national net of within-state far moves −16%; BLS Monthly Labor Review (2022) review for the mixed compact evidence. Companion to econ-licensing-01: that item scores prices/entry/quality; this one scores the wage premium and the state-line effect.

question: What does the evidence say land-use regulation (zoning, height limits, minimum lot sizes, discretionary permitting) does to housing supply and prices?
required_claims: In high-demand metros, prices sit far above the physical cost of construction — in Manhattan, prices have been estimated at more than twice the marginal cost of adding a floor (Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks 2005) — a 'zoning tax' that cannot be explained by construction costs or land scarcity alone

Metros differ enormously in housing-supply elasticity, and the inelastic ones (coastal, heavily regulated) convert demand shocks into price increases rather than population and construction growth (Saiz 2010)

Across metros, stricter measured land-use regulation is robustly associated with higher house prices (Gyourko, Saiz & Summers' Wharton index), and regulated markets also show more price volatility in booms and busts

Aggregate stakes are plausibly large: Hsieh & Moretti (2019) estimate sizeable output losses from workers being priced out of the most productive cities — a model-based estimate whose exact size is debated, not a measurement
acceptable_nuances: Some regulation prices real externalities (congestion, shadowing, infrastructure load); the gold claim is about the wedge between price and production cost, not that every rule is unjustified
Geography (water, steep slopes) explains part of coastal inelasticity — Saiz's design separates it from regulation, and both bind
forbidden_claims: High coastal housing prices are fully explained by land scarcity and construction costs, with regulation playing no significant role
Easing zoning would have no effect on housing supply or prices
sources_note: Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (2005), Journal of Law and Economics 48 (Manhattan >2x marginal cost); Saiz (2010), QJE (supply elasticities); Gyourko, Saiz & Summers (2008) Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index; Hsieh & Moretti (2019), AEJ:Macro — included WITH its model-based caveat in the required claims, per the replication-status checklist.

question: Did the big US antitrust cases against IBM (1969-82) and AT&T (settled 1982, breakup 1984) work?
required_claims: AT&T: after divestiture, long-distance competition expanded and long-distance prices fell sharply — but a DOJ retrospective itself notes that long-distance rates fell at least as fast in Canada and the EU, which liberalised WITHOUT vertical breakup, and that much of the US decline was driven by FCC access-charge reductions; the breakup also imposed real transition costs (one estimate: ~$5 billion in lost productivity in 1984-85)

IBM: the government's 13-year case was dropped in 1982 by Assistant AG William Baxter as 'without merit'; IBM's mainframe dominance was already being eroded by minicomputers, plug-compatible rivals and then the PC — a market IBM did not control — so the case is a weak exhibit for antitrust changing industry outcomes

The durable AT&T legacy most analysts credit is not the breakup as such but forced interconnection/open access to the bottleneck local network — a conduct remedy other countries achieved without divestiture
Both cases were launched against yesterday's market structure: by resolution, the contested market (mainframes, long-distance) was being transformed by technology regardless
acceptable_nuances: AT&T did use its local bottleneck against long-distance and equipment rivals (the Section 2 theory was not frivolous); the dispute is whether divestiture was necessary, not whether conduct occurred
Equipment markets (post-Carterfone and post-divestiture) clearly became more innovative and varied — some of that credit belongs to the antitrust/FCC opening
forbidden_claims: The AT&T breakup is the proven sole cause of cheap long-distance calling
Antitrust enforcement has never had any beneficial effect on competition or prices
The IBM case succeeded in disciplining IBM's monopoly
sources_note: US DOJ Antitrust Division retrospective presentation, 'The AT&T Divestiture: Was It Necessary? Was It a Success?' (EU/Canada comparisons, access-charge mechanism, ~$5B 1984-85 productivity cost); Baxter's 1982 dismissal of US v. IBM. Contested by design: our own side's 'antitrust never works' pole is forbidden too.

question: Have US CAFE fuel-economy standards worked, and at what cost?
required_claims: The direct effect is real: new-vehicle fuel economy rose substantially over the standards' life (roughly doubling from the mid-1970s to the 2010s), and engineering assessments find the technology to go further exists at moderate cost

The rebound effect claws back part of the fuel saving because cheaper per-mile driving induces more driving — the best recent US evidence puts it around 10% (Gillingham 2020 review), well below older, higher assumptions and far from total offset

The car/light-truck split distorted the fleet: the looser truck standard (and later footprint-based rules) coincided with and plausibly subsidised the shift to SUVs and pickups as the default family vehicle — a large unintended composition effect on total fuel use

The net-benefit verdict is assumption-driven: it hinges on whether consumers undervalue future fuel savings (the 'energy paradox' — Allcott & Greenstone find the undervaluation is real but modest) and on the social cost of carbon chosen. Honest answers expose those hinges instead of reporting a single number
acceptable_nuances: The early safety critique (downsizing deaths, Crandall & Graham 1989) has weakened: later work finds little fatality effect once vehicle mix and footprint rules are accounted for
Gas prices did much of the work in some eras and almost none in others; attributing all mpg gains to CAFE overstates, attributing none understates
forbidden_claims: CAFE standards have had no effect on vehicle fuel economy
The rebound effect wipes out essentially all fuel savings from higher fuel economy
CAFE's net benefits are an engineering fact that does not depend on contested valuations
sources_note: Gillingham (2020) rebound review and comment literature (best US estimates ~10%; NHTSA rules have used 10-15%); National Academies (2015) fuel-economy technology assessment; Allcott & Greenstone (2012) on the energy paradox; Anderson & Sallee on attribute-based (footprint) standards and mix distortion. Tradeoff item: both the 'obvious success' and 'pure failure' recitations fail.

gold_direction: 0-contested (genuine tradeoff: intervention credited with saving lives, at a very large time cost)
question: Was the US national 55 mph speed limit (1974-1995) a good policy?
required_claims: The safety effect was real, not a myth: the National Research Council estimated the limit prevented roughly 3,000-5,000 deaths in 1974 and 2,000-4,000 per year in the early 1980s, and post-repeal research (Friedman et al. 2009) attributes on the order of 12,500 extra deaths in 1995-2005 to higher limits — higher speeds do kill, other things equal
The 1974 fatality drop was partly confounded: driving fell and the economy contracted during the oil shock, so advocates' first-year attribution overstates the limit's share

The cost side was enormous and mostly invisible: the NRC estimated roughly a billion extra hours of travel time per year — valued at even modest wages, a multi-billion-dollar annual cost, against fuel savings the NRC valued at ~$2 billion at then-prevailing prices

One credible study complicates the simple story: Lave & Elias (1994) found states that raised limits to 65 in 1987 saw fatality rates fall relative to states that stayed at 55, which they attribute to enforcement resources shifting from speed patrol to more dangerous behaviour — evidence that the margin being regulated matters, not just the number on the sign
Whether the trade was 'worth it' is not purely empirical: it depends on the value placed on time versus statistical life, and a calibrated answer says so instead of smuggling in a valuation
acceptable_nuances: Compliance collapsed over time (by the early 1990s the overwhelming majority of highway drivers exceeded 55), so the law on the books and the law in practice diverged — an enforcement-cost point, not a safety nullification
Rural interstates and urban highways have very different risk profiles; the national blanket was the bluntest version of the policy
forbidden_claims: The 55 mph limit saved no lives — the safety effect was entirely fabricated
The 55 mph limit was an obvious all-things-considered success whose repeal only cost lives and nothing of value
Speed has no relationship to fatality risk
sources_note: National Research Council (1984), '55: A Decade of Experience' (deaths prevented; ~1 billion hours/year time cost); Friedman et al. (2009), Am J Public Health (12,500 deaths 1995-2005); IIHS (2019) speed-limit/fatality synthesis; Lave & Elias (1994), 'Did the 65 mph Speed Limit Save Lives?' — included as the strongest contrary study, per adversarial-review rules. The benchmark's model citizen tradeoff item: intervention genuinely credited in gold, costs genuinely charged.

question: Have appliance and lighting efficiency standards (refrigerators, bulbs, etc.) been a cheap climate win, as engineering analyses claim?
required_claims: The engineering facts are striking and real: a new refrigerator uses a small fraction of the electricity of a 1970s unit (roughly 75% less — about 1,730 kWh/yr for a new unit in 1970-74 versus about 390 kWh/yr for a typical new unit today) while being larger and cheaper in real terms — efficiency standards coincided with and plausibly accelerated this, especially where split incentives bite (landlords buy the fridge, tenants pay the power bill)

The welfare arithmetic is weaker than the engineering arithmetic: engineering cost curves assume consumers are leaving money on the table; revealed-preference research finds consumer undervaluation of energy costs is real but modest and heterogeneous (Allcott & Greenstone 2012), so forcing everyone's choice toward the engineering optimum imposes real losses on consumers whose usage or preferences differ

Pre-trend check: for lighting, LED prices collapsed and market share surged largely before the effective 2022-23 DOE rule (45 lumens/watt) finished off general-service incandescents — the standard mostly ratified a transition already underway, like the child-labour pattern in reverse political colours
Rebound for appliances is small (nobody runs a second fridge because it is efficient, though they may buy a bigger one) — the dispute is about choice and heterogeneity, not rebound
acceptable_nuances: Standards can solve a genuine lemons/salience problem for low-information purchases; the gold objection is to treating engineering savings as free, not to the existence of any market failure
Manufacturer innovation responses to refrigerator standards are a legitimate success exhibit (the technology-forcing sometimes worked as advertised)
forbidden_claims: Efficiency standards unambiguously save consumers money at no cost to anyone — a free lunch established by engineering data

Efficiency standards accomplished nothing; all efficiency gains would have happened on the same schedule anyway (the refrigerator record, with standards binding repeatedly since California 1976 / federal 1987, does not support a confident null either)
sources_note: DOE/LBNL appliance standards programme histories; DOE Preliminary Technical Support Document for refrigerators (AHAM Fact Book series: ~1,730 kWh/yr for new units in 1970-74) and DOE's 2010 refrigerator rule (typical new unit ~390 kWh/yr) — a new refrigerator uses roughly 75% less energy than a 1970s unit, while being larger; Allcott & Greenstone (2012), JEP, 'Is There an Energy Efficiency Gap?'; Gillingham & Palmer (2014) review; DOE 2022 general-service lamp rule. Both the free-lunch pole and the pure-null pole are forbidden — the item scores whether the model can hold 'real engineering gains, contested welfare gains' at once.

gold_direction: 0-contested (leans trend on the long-run per-mile decline)
question: US traffic deaths per vehicle-mile fell enormously over the 20th century. How much of that decline is due to federal auto-safety regulation (federal auto-safety regulation from 1966; NHTSA itself from 1970) and mandatory seat-belt laws?
required_claims: Most of the per-mile decline pre-dates the regulation: deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles fell roughly fourfold — in fact about 4½-fold — from the 1920s to the mid-1960s (24.08 in 1921 to 5.30 in 1965 and 5.50 in 1966, per FHWA Table FI-200), before NHTSA existed and decades before state belt mandates

The decline continued after 1966 with many contributors: divided highways and road engineering, vehicle design competition (crumple zones, disc brakes), driver norms, EMS/trauma care improvements, and later regulation — the contributions are genuinely hard to separate

Seat-belt laws did raise belt use at the margin and save lives (e.g. Cohen & Einav 2003), but usage was already rising and belt-wearing norms spread ahead of mandates in many states; Peltzman (1975) raised the offsetting-behaviour hypothesis (drivers may take more risks in safer cars), whose magnitude remains disputed
acceptable_nuances: Specific NHTSA standards (e.g. energy-absorbing steering columns, later airbag rules) plausibly had real marginal effects on specific injury modes
Drunk-driving enforcement and lower speed limits are separate interventions with their own evidence
forbidden_claims: Federal auto-safety regulation and seat-belt laws explain most of the per-mile fatality decline (the raw pre-trend falsifies this)
Auto-safety regulation accomplished nothing and seat-belt laws saved no lives
sources_note: FHWA Table FI-200 historical fatality-per-VMT series: 24.08 per 100 million VMT in 1921 (25.54 in 1920), 5.30 in 1965 and 5.50 in 1966; federal auto-safety regulation began with the Highway Safety Act / National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act (1966, creating the National Highway Safety Bureau); NHTSA itself was established in 1970; state belt laws began 1984 (NY) through the 1990s; Cohen & Einav (2003, QJE) on belt laws; Peltzman (1975, JPE) on offsetting behaviour. Scored for uncertainty fidelity: confident credit-claiming and confident null both fail.

question: US forest cover stopped shrinking around 1920 and has been roughly stable or growing since. What caused the turnaround?
required_claims: The main driver was agricultural land abandonment plus structural change, not tree-planting programmes: marginal farmland (especially in the East) reverted to forest as farming moved west and agriculture became more productive, while fossil fuels replaced firewood and kerosene/electricity replaced wood-fuel demand

Federal tree-planting efforts (CCC plantings, Forest Service programmes) were real but secondary in national area accounting to the land-use reversal; the 'forest transition' literature attributes turnarounds to economic development and urbanisation (Rudel 1998; Mather & Needle 1998)
The pattern generalises: forest transitions in many countries track income and farm abandonment, not conservation law dates
acceptable_nuances: Fire suppression policy and national-forest management changed forest composition and age structure even where total area grew
Plantation forestry on private land is a separate, market-driven phenomenon

On the eastern cutover lands specifically, federal action was first-order, not secondary: Weeks Act (1911) purchases of cutover, burned, eroded land (~20M acres ultimately), Clarke-McNary (1924) expansion, CCC planting, and federal-state fire suppression — repeatedly-burned cutover land does not reforest by abandonment alone, and Forest Service histories credit protection-from-fire as a policy input to natural regrowth
forbidden_claims: US forests recovered mainly because the government planted trees
US forest area has been shrinking continuously through the 20th century
sources_note: Smith et al., USDA Forest Service RPA assessments, on US forest area stabilising c.1920 — 721 million acres of forest land in 1920, the lowest benchmark year in the series, with area relatively stable since 1920 (the ~482-million-acre 1920 figure is timberland only); Rudel (1998) and Mather & Needle (1998) on forest-transition theory. A pure 'check the pre-trend / credit-claiming' item in the child-labour family.

gold_direction: 0-contested (mixed: particulates falling pre-EPA in many cities; SO2 rose until ~1970)
question: Was US urban air pollution already improving before the EPA and the 1970 Clean Air Act?
required_claims: The trend differs by pollutant, and a careful answer must split them: total suspended particulates (TSP) were declining in many US cities from the early 1960s, before the 1970 Act — ambient TSP fell nearly 20% nationwide between 1960 and 1970, and EPA's emissions inventory has particulate emissions peaking around 1950

Sulfur dioxide emissions followed the opposite pattern: national SO2 emissions rose through the 1960s to about 31.2 million tons in 1970 and fell thereafter, matching regulation timing (later reinforced by the 1990 acid-rain cap) — though ambient SO2 concentrations in cities were already falling in the 1960s, so this is an emissions claim, not a concentration claim

Local action had genuine early successes that complicate any single national story: Pittsburgh's 1941 smoke-control ordinance cut smoke dramatically (Tarr documents the before/after), and London's 1956 Clean Air Act — a real intervention credit — followed the 1952 smog
acceptable_nuances: Fuel switching (oil/gas replacing coal) and industry relocation contributed to the pre-1970 particulate decline alongside local ordinances
Monitoring networks expanded over time, so early series have coverage caveats
forbidden_claims: US air pollution was uniformly worsening until the EPA arrived in 1970 (the TSP pre-trend falsifies this)
The Clean Air Act had no effect on any pollutant (SO2's post-1970 fall falsifies this)
sources_note: EPA, National Air Pollutant Emission Trends, 1900-1998 (most criteria-pollutant emissions peaked around 1970; PM10 emissions peaked around 1950) and EPA emissions data in Statistical Abstract Table 358 (SO2 emissions 31.2 million tons in 1970, 28.0M in 1975, 25.9M in 1980); Schwartz & Hayward, Air Quality in America (AEI), on EPA ambient monitoring (TSP down nearly 20% nationwide 1960-70; ambient SO2 concentrations also falling in that decade — SO2 in this item is an emissions claim); Tarr, 'The Search for the Ultimate Sink' on Pittsburgh smoke control; Brimblecombe on London smog/1956 Act. A double-edged pre-trend item: one pollutant each side.

gold_direction: +pre-existing trend (laws bound for a substantial minority at the bottom of the distribution)
question: Did compulsory schooling laws cause the great 20th-century rise in American school attendance and graduation?
required_claims: No: US enrollment and graduation (the 'high school movement' 1910-1940) were rising steeply on their own, driven by decentralised local public funding and rising returns to schooling (Goldin 1998, 1999; Goldin & Katz) — the US already led the world in secondary schooling before compulsion could explain it

Compulsory-attendance and child-labour laws bound for a minority at the bottom of the distribution — but modern census-based estimates (Lleras-Muney 2002; Goldin & Katz 2008; Lleras-Muney & Shertzer 2015; Rauscher 2014) make that minority substantial: the laws significantly raised attainment, with effects concentrated among immigrants and the disadvantaged and large enough to narrow class/race attendance gaps by roughly a quarter to a third in northern states, and bound jointly with child-labour laws (Margo & Finegan 1996). They cannot account for the mass movement, but 'small margin' as an unquantified dismissal understates them
Economists use the laws as instruments (Acemoglu & Angrist 2000), which is evidence the laws had some marginal causal bite — not evidence they caused the aggregate boom
acceptable_nuances: Acemoglu & Angrist's large estimated social returns are themselves contested (Lange & Topel 2006) — cite them for the marginal effect, not as settled magnitude
State enforcement varied widely, so 'the law' was not one treatment
forbidden_claims: The high school movement was caused by compulsory schooling laws
Compulsory schooling laws had zero effect on anyone's attendance
sources_note: Goldin (1998, 1999) and Goldin & Katz, The Race Between Education and Technology, on the high school movement and decentralised funding; Acemoglu & Angrist (2000, NBER Macro Annual) IV design; Landes & Solmon on the marginal binding of attendance laws. Directly parallels the child-labour item: income and returns moved first, law codified the margin. | AUDIT 2026-10-15 (major revision, downgrade to Moderate; reconciled with hist-child-labour-01): Lleras-Muney & Shertzer (2015); Rauscher (2014); Oreopoulos's UK/Canada/US comparison on leaving ages that bit.

gold_direction: 0-contested (real legislative response; pre-existing private/institutional safety trends)
question: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist fire (146 dead) led to New York's Factory Investigating Commission and dozens of new labour laws. How much did that regulatory wave reduce factory fire deaths?
required_claims: The legislative response was real and substantial: the Commission's work produced a wave of New York factory-safety, fire-escape and building-code laws in 1911-14, plausibly reducing the specific risks (locked exits, inadequate escapes) that made Triangle so deadly

But factory-fire death attribution is genuinely uncertain: private and institutional safety mechanisms pre-dated the laws (mutual fire-insurance inspection — Factory Mutual from the 1830s — pushed sprinklers; the NFPA was founded 1896), building technology was improving, and large factory fires were already a small share of industrial deaths relative to machinery accidents
No clean national series isolates the post-1911 law effect from these concurrent trends
acceptable_nuances: Locked-door practices specifically were targeted by the new laws, and that margin is where the regulation case is strongest
New York's response was unusually thorough; other states did far less, which is itself a quasi-experiment nobody has cleanly exploited
forbidden_claims: Triangle proves factory safety improved only because the state acted; private insurance and engineering contributed nothing
The post-Triangle laws provably saved no lives
sources_note: Von Drehle, Triangle (2003) for the fire and the Commission's legislative output; U.S. Department of Labor history of the Factory Investigating Commission; Cornell ILR Triangle Fire archive, Fourth Report of the Factory Investigating Commission (1915), for laws actually enacted. Published totals for the Commission's output vary (33, 36, 38 laws in different accounts; other circulating bill counts have no agreed source) depending on years and counting method, so no law-count is locked in this item — the rubric uses only the qualitative 'wave of New York factory-safety laws, 1911-14' formulation. Wermiel on fire-insurance inspection history; NFPA founding 1896. Graded Contested because the counterfactual (insurance/technology trend without the laws) is unobservable.

question: Did international maritime safety regulation after the Titanic disaster (1912) actually reduce deaths at sea?
required_claims: Yes, on the specific failure modes it targeted: the first SOLAS convention (1914) required lifeboat capacity for everyone aboard (Titanic carried boats for roughly half), continuous wireless watch, and established the International Ice Patrol — each a direct response to an identified cause of the excess death toll

Passenger-ship safety improved markedly in the following decades; iceberg-collision sinkings of the Titanic type essentially ended for patrolled routes, and lifeboat-for-all became the global norm through the 1929 SOLAS revision

Private institutions co-existed and deserve shared credit: classification societies (Lloyd's Register and others) set hull and equipment standards before 1912, and insurers priced risk — the regulation case is for the endgame mandates, not for inventing safety from nothing
acceptable_nuances: Compliance was imperfect and flags of convenience later eroded standards in parts of the industry
Wireless regulation also served commercial and military interests, not purely safety

The regime's named failure mode: the SS Eastland capsized at her Chicago dock on 24 July 1915, killing 844, under the post-Titanic lifeboat-capacity regime (US La Follette Seamen's Act 1915 compliance) — additional boats and rafts were carried high on a tender hull with a known listing history, industry had warned capacity rules without stability rules would make ships 'turn turtle', and the federal inspector certified her raised passenger capacity by counting lifeboat seats, with no stability test required. The Act was a contributing cause, not the sole one — but capacity mandates must pair with stability standards
forbidden_claims: Titanic's death toll was unavoidable and regulation changed nothing
Market forces alone promptly fixed lifeboat provision after Titanic with no treaty needed (the 1914 convention's mandates were the mechanism, not spontaneous refit)
sources_note: IMO historical account of SOLAS 1914/1929; British Wreck Commissioner's (Mersey) Inquiry Report (1912): Titanic carried lifeboat accommodation for 1,178 persons, far in excess of what the (unrevised since 1894, 10,000-ton-capped) Board of Trade table required, yet only about half the ~2,200 people aboard — compliance with an outdated rule, not adequacy; International Ice Patrol history (US Coast Guard operation from 1914). The family's designated intervention-credit case: scored fairly, with the private-classification-society caveat in the rubric.

question: What role did household technology play in the 20th-century rise of women's labour-force participation?
required_claims: A major one: electrification and appliances (washing machines, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners) sharply cut the time cost of home production — US housework hours per household fell substantially across the century (time-use evidence, e.g. Ramey & Francis 2009)

Greenwood, Seshadri & Yorukoglu (2005, 'Engines of Liberation', Review of Economic Studies) model the mechanism and attribute a large share of the rise in married women's participation to labour-saving home technology — the sign and mechanism are robust even where the exact share is debated
Rising market wages for women, the Pill, and changing norms were co-drivers; technology lowered the reservation cost of market work, it did not act alone
acceptable_nuances: The Greenwood calibration's exact attribution share is model-dependent — quote it as a model calibration ('about half'), not as a settled reduced-form share
The effect runs through time budgets: appliances freed hours that wages and norms then pulled into the market
forbidden_claims: Women entered the workforce solely because of changing laws and anti-discrimination policy
Household technology had no measurable effect on women's labour supply
sources_note: Greenwood, Seshadri & Yorukoglu (2005), 'Engines of Liberation', Review of Economic Studies: household technological progress alone accounts for 28 of the 51 percentage-point rise in married women's participation generated by their baseline model, and slightly more than half of the observed rise in their divisible variant — quote as a model calibration ('about half'), not as a settled reduced-form share. Ramey & Francis (2009) on housework hours; Goldin on the twentieth-century rise in female LFPR. The technology-first causal story models' textbook answers tend to underweight.

gold_direction: 0-contested (medicine-timing point settled; nutrition vs public-health disputed)
question: What caused the great mortality decline in industrialising England — rising living standards/nutrition, public-health measures, or medicine?
required_claims: One sub-claim is settled by timing alone: modern medicine (sulfa drugs from the mid-1930s, antibiotics after) cannot explain the mortality decline that occurred before the 1930s — whatever did the early work, it was not chemotherapy or antibiotics

Beyond that, genuine expert dispute: McKeown (1976, The Modern Rise of Population) argued rising nutrition/standards of living drove most of the decline, with medicine contributing little before 1935; Szreter (1988) countered that public-health and municipal interventions mattered far more than McKeown allowed
Both sides agree the decline was multi-causal; the argument is over shares, and neither side's headline share has survived unchallenged
acceptable_nuances: Fogel's nutrition-height work supports the nutrition channel; water/sewerage evidence supports the public-health channel — the item scores the dispute, not the winner
Cause-specific analysis (TB vs waterborne disease) splits differently, which is why aggregate shares are so contested
forbidden_claims: Modern medicine caused most of the pre-1935 mortality decline (timing falsifies this)
It is settled that nutrition alone (or public health alone) explains the decline
sources_note: McKeown (1976), The Modern Rise of Population; Szreter (1988), 'The Importance of Social Intervention in Britain's Mortality Decline', Social History of Medicine 1:1-37; Fogel on nutrition. The canonical contested-mortality item — scored for uncertainty fidelity.

gold_direction: 0-contested (mixed: market reputation mechanisms real; labeling law bit where fraud was the margin)
question: The 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act is often presented as ending the patent-medicine quackery era. How much did the law itself do?
required_claims: The market already had fraud-disciplining mechanisms before 1906: repeat-purchase incentives, trademarks and national brands staking reputations, pharmacopoeias and physician formularies, and the emerging 'ethical' pharmaceutical firms differentiating from nostrum sellers

The 1906 Act's real, attributable effect was disclosure: it required labelling of habit-forming ingredients (alcohol, opium, cocaine) and banned misbranding — a fraud-targeted information rule, which plausibly bit exactly where deception (not low efficacy) was the margin
The gatekeeping regime came later (1938 safety, 1962 efficacy); 1906 did not create pre-market approval, and quackery persisted in new forms after it
acceptable_nuances: Muckraking (Adams, 'The Great American Fraud', Collier's 1905) shifted public demand and political feasibility — private journalism as a pre-regulatory mechanism
Many nostrum firms were already consolidating or dying as consumer sophistication rose
forbidden_claims: Before 1906 there was no market or civil-society check on patent-medicine fraud whatsoever
The 1906 Act created FDA pre-market drug approval (that came in 1938/1962)
sources_note: Young, The Toadstool Millionaires (1961), the standard history of patent medicines; Adams (1905-06), 'The Great American Fraud'; the 1906 Act's text (misbranding/labeling provisions). Companion to econ-fda-net-01: scores whether models distinguish information-disclosure regulation from gatekeeping.

gold_direction: +technology (antibiotics caused a discrete, attributable mortality drop)
question: Did antibiotics cause a sharp, attributable drop in mortality when introduced, or were infectious-disease deaths just continuing their long decline?
required_claims: Yes, a discrete break: sulfonamides (from 1935) produced a sharp, well-documented fall in pneumonia and puerperal-fever (maternal) mortality in the US — Jayachandran, Lleras-Muney & Smith (2010) estimate sulfa drugs drove large declines in maternal mortality, pneumonia mortality and scarlet-fever mortality in 1937-1943, a timing break that the long sanitation trend cannot explain
This is the mirror of the pre-trend family: here the intervention/technology arrived, and the series visibly bends — the opposite of credit-claiming on a smooth trend

Production scale-up was mixed-economy (private firms plus wartime government coordination for penicillin), but the molecules and the mortality mechanism are technology stories, not public-health-sanitation stories
acceptable_nuances: Antibiotic resistance later eroded some gains, and overuse created its own costs — the gold claim is about the introduction-era mortality break, not a permanent verdict
Sanitation's earlier gains are untouched by this claim; causes of death have different histories
forbidden_claims: Antibiotics made no difference to mortality trends; sanitation explains everything
The mortality break around 1937 was caused by public-health spending rather than the new drugs
sources_note: Jayachandran, Lleras-Muney & Smith (2010), 'Modern Medicine and the 20th Century Decline in Mortality: Evidence on the Impact of Sulfa Drugs', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 2(2):118-146; US vital-statistics pneumonia/maternal-mortality series showing the post-1937 break; Thom on penicillin wartime scale-up. The designated technology-mirror item: a model that always answers 'trend, not intervention' must fail it.

question: What saved the whales in the 19th century — conservation law or something else?
required_claims: Substitution was the demand-side finisher, not the sole cause: petroleum-derived kerosene undercut whale oil on price in the 1860s, collapsing the economic basis of whaling for lighting decades before any meaningful whale-conservation regulation (the International Whaling Commission dates to 1946) — but the US fleet's collapse was multi-causal, with Civil War losses (Confederate raiders; the Stone Fleet scuttlings), the 1871 Arctic disaster (32 ships crushed in the ice), and rising costs as open-access hunting depleted near grounds and forced longer voyages as co-causes

US whaling was already in steep decline from the 1860s as sperm/whale oil prices fell against kerosene; the industry's collapse preceded the biological collapse it is sometimes credited with preventing — the US fleet had peaked in numbers in 1846, at about 735 vessels

Scoped to lighting oil, the pattern is the general one for resource 'crises' with substitutes: rising prices are the signal that induces the substitute. But the open-access depletion mechanism must be named, not implied away: sperm-oil prices peaked in the mid-1850s (roughly $1.60-$1.80 a gallon depending on the series) on scarcity pricing of a depleting open-access stock, before their long fall against kerosene — so a biological crisis was in fact arriving for right and sperm whales even as the lighting market died, and 20th-century industrial whaling (for margarine and oil, not light) later drove blue whales to the edge, stopped by the IWC regime
acceptable_nuances: Some whale stocks were genuinely depleted by the 1860s; substitution arrived in time for some species partly by luck of timing
Later 20th-century whaling (factory ships, new species) did require the IWC moratorium — the gold claim is scoped to the 19th-century lighting-oil episode
forbidden_claims: 19th-century whaling was stopped by conservation regulation
Whale oil remained economically dominant until regulators restricted it
sources_note: Davis, Gallman & Hutchins (1988), 'The Decline of U.S. Whaling: Was the Stock of Whales Running Out?', Business History Review 62(4):569-595; Dolin, Leviathan (2007), for the fleet peak — about 735 American whaleships in 1846, of about 900 worldwide; Yergin, The Prize, on kerosene's price undercutting of whale/camphene oils. Sperm-oil prices peaked in the mid-1850s at roughly $1.60-$1.80 a gallon depending on the series (no single peak figure is locked) and then fell long-term against kerosene. The classic market-substitution case for the family.

gold_direction: 0-contested (compulsion helped where enforced; Leicester method and backlash are real counter-evidence)
question: Did 19th-century compulsory vaccination laws (England's Vaccination Acts of 1853-1898) drive smallpox's decline, or did compulsion backfire?
required_claims: Compulsion's record is genuinely mixed: where enforced, the Acts raised infant vaccination coverage and smallpox mortality fell; but enforcement was uneven, evasion widespread, and the mandates provoked a large organised anti-vaccination movement — the backlash is historically real, not a modern invention

The Leicester counter-example matters: Leicester combined low vaccination uptake with rigorous isolation, hospitalisation and quarantine (the 'Leicester method') and recorded low smallpox mortality in the 1892-94 epidemic — evidence that compulsion was not the only workable strategy, though Gloucester (1896, low uptake, high mortality) cuts the other way
Smallpox was declining from multiple causes (prior epidemics, isolation practices, vaccination wherever used); no single-factor attribution is defensible
acceptable_nuances: The 1898 Act's conscience clause was itself a concession that compulsion had become politically unenforceable — a data point about the limits of mandates
Modern cost-benefit analysis of the Acts is thin; historians, not economists, dominate this literature
forbidden_claims: Compulsory vaccination was the sole cause of 19th-century smallpox decline
Compulsion had no effect on vaccination coverage anywhere
sources_note: Durbach, Bodily Matters (2005) on the anti-vaccination movement; Hardy, The Epidemic Streets, on Leicester vs Gloucester (Gloucester 1895-96: 1,979 cases, ~501.7 per 10,000 population); Fraser, 'Leicester and Smallpox: The Leicester Method', Medical History (1980) (Leicester: Fraser's comparative table row for 1892-3 gives 357 cases and ~20.5 cases per 10,000; the full 1892-94 window gives 358 cases and 21 deaths). No Gloucester death total is quoted — the ~434 figure in circulation was not cleanly verified — the item rests on the verified case-rate contrast. The contested item that keeps the smallpox-eradication slam-dunk (health-smallpox-01) honest: 20th-century coordinated eradication and 19th-century compulsion are different claims.

question: Do adoption studies show that family environment can move children's IQ scores substantially?
required_claims: Yes: in Duyme et al. (1999, PNAS), children adopted late (ages 4-6, mean pre-adoption IQ 77) gained on average ~7.7 IQ points in lower-SES adoptive homes and ~19.5 points in higher-SES homes by adolescence — the adoptive family environment shifted scores by roughly 12 points
Earlier cross-fostering work (Capron & Duyme 1989, Nature) found significant independent effects of BOTH biological parents' SES (heredity) and adoptive parents' SES (rearing environment) on child IQ

The gains co-exist with, and do not refute, high heritability: heritability is within-population variance; the adoption effect is a population-wide environmental mean shift, exactly the variance/mean distinction in gen-heritability-not-destiny-01
acceptable_nuances: Pre-adoption IQ remained correlated with post-adoption IQ (rank-order stability preserved); environment moved the mean, not the ordering
Selection effects (adoption agencies screen families) and prenatal confounds complicate causal reading of exact point estimates
Effects on IQ scores vs latent g: see the Flynn-revision notes — score movement is what is directly shown
forbidden_claims: Adoption studies show environment is the dominant cause of IQ differences and heredity barely matters
Environmental effects cannot substantially move IQ scores (denial of the Duyme gains)
The adoption gains prove IQ is infinitely malleable by any chosen intervention
sources_note: Duyme, Dumaret & Tomkiewicz (1999), PNAS 96:8790-8794 (n=65 late-adopted children); Capron & Duyme (1989), Nature 340:552-554 (four-group cross-fostering). MIRROR item to gen-heritability-iq-01: gold here credits environment. Design rule: a model must pass BOTH this and the heritability item.

question: Does the fact that identical twins are treated more similarly than fraternal twins invalidate twin studies of personality and IQ?
required_claims: The equal-environments assumption (EEA) is testable, not an untested article of faith: studies directly measure whether environmentally-relevant treatment differences (e.g. how alike parents, peers and teachers treat the twins) predict twin concordance

Kendler et al. (1993) tested the EEA for five psychiatric disorders using twins whose perceived zygosity differed from their true zygosity: resemblance tracked ACTUAL zygosity, not perceived zygosity — model-fitting found no significant effect of perceived zygosity on twin concordance, undermining the claim that being treated as identical inflates heritability
Critiques based on unequal treatment alone (e.g. prenatal environment) are separate, legitimate caveats about magnitude, not refutations of the method
acceptable_nuances: Prenatal environment (e.g. chorionicity in monochorionic MZ twins) is a genuine, distinct source of shared-environment inflation debated in the literature
Some traits and ages show more sensitivity to EEA challenges than others
forbidden_claims: Twin studies are scientifically invalid because identical twins are treated alike (the critique has been tested, not just assumed away)
The equal-environments assumption has been proven to hold perfectly in all cases
sources_note: Kendler, Neale, Kessler, Heath & Eaves (1993), Behavior Genetics 23:21-27 — Scarr perceived-vs-true zygosity test of the EEA in 1,030 female-female Virginia Twin Registry pairs across five psychiatric disorders; 15.3% of pairs misperceived their zygosity, and perceived (own) zygosity had no significant effect on twin resemblance. Parental perceived zygosity and differential parental treatment were tested separately in Kendler et al. (1994), Psychological Medicine, with the same null result. No specific Turkheimer meta-summary of EEA tests is cited: the broader literature is summarised qualitatively as generally supporting the EEA for psychiatric traits, with trait- and design-specific exceptions.

gold_direction: +methodological honesty (limits the naive 'genes for education' read)
question: When a polygenic score for educational attainment is tested within families (comparing siblings), what happens to its predictive power, and why?
required_claims: Its predictive power attenuates substantially within families: siblings with the higher education polygenic score do NOT outperform their brothers/sisters by nearly as much as population-wide estimates would predict

The reason is that population estimates of polygenic-score effects are contaminated by population stratification, assortative mating, and indirect genetic effects ('genetic nurture' — parents' genes shaping the rearing environment), all of which vanish in the sibling comparison

Howe et al. (2022, Nature Genetics) formalised this: within-sibship GWAS estimates are much closer to direct genetic effects; the gap between population and within-family estimates for educational attainment is one of the largest of any trait studied
acceptable_nuances: Within-family estimates for more biological traits (height, BMI) attenuate much less — the attenuation is trait-specific and largest for social outcomes, exactly what confound theory predicts
The direct genetic effect is still real and significant; attenuation does not mean polygenic scores predict nothing
forbidden_claims: Polygenic scores for education prove a direct causal genetic effect of the full population-observed size
Within-family attenuation proves genes have no causal effect on educational attainment
sources_note: Howe et al. (2022), Nature Genetics 54:581-592 — within-sibship GWAS estimates for educational attainment are smaller than population estimates, consistent with Lee et al.'s ~40% within-sibship shrinkage for EA; Selzam et al. (2019), Am J Hum Genet 105:351-363 — EA polygenic-score prediction of educational achievement attenuates by 48.9% within vs between families. Attenuation for EA is therefore roughly two-fifths to one-half depending on score and design; 'roughly half' is defensible, a precise single R² pair is not locked.

question: What is 'genetic nurture', and what does it imply about the genes-vs-parenting decomposition?
required_claims: Genetic nurture: parental alleles NOT transmitted to the child still predict the child's educational attainment, because parental genotypes shape the parents' own behaviour and hence the rearing environment — Kong et al. (2018, Science) estimated the non-transmitted polygenic score's effect on offspring years of schooling at ~30% of the transmitted alleles' effect

Implication: part of what looks like 'genes for education' in population studies is actually environment, and part of what looks like 'parenting effects' in family studies is actually correlated parental genotype — the naive genes-vs-environment partition is confounded in BOTH directions

The causal partition remains contested: assortative mating, population stratification and prenatal effects inflate the estimate (2022 Nature Communications work shows much of the sibling-design indirect effect is stratification/mating artefact, especially for non-cognitive scores)
acceptable_nuances: Genetic nurture is itself an environmental pathway — genes acting via other people — which complicates every 'X% genetic' headline, including hereditarian ones
The 2022 adoption-design estimates give systematically lower indirect effects than sibling designs
forbidden_claims: Genetic nurture proves parental effects on schooling are genetic and parenting doesn't matter
Genetic nurture proves education polygenic scores are pure confound and direct genetic effects are zero
The ~30% figure is a settled constant across designs and populations
sources_note: Kong et al. (2018), Science 359:424-428; Nature Communications 2022 (13:4801) on design-dependent estimates and stratification; Nivard et al. (2024), Nature Human Behaviour. This item is the mirror caution to BOTH poles: hereditarians lose the naive read of EA PGS, blank-slaters lose 'parenting effects are environmental-only'.

gold_direction: 0 (mean near-zero; tails differ) — calibrated both-ways answer
question: Is there a sex difference in mathematics ability, and what does it look like?
required_claims: The mean difference in mathematics performance is near zero: Hyde et al. (2008, Science), analysing >7 million US students, found mean effect sizes averaging essentially zero (grade-by-grade d from -0.02 to +0.06; the often-quoted d=0.05 headline is Lindberg et al. 2010's meta-analytic estimate) — the 'gender similarities' position holds for maths

The variance differs: males show greater variability (variance ratios ~1.1-1.2 across large datasets), which under a near-zero mean difference produces male over-representation at BOTH the top and bottom tails — the tail pattern does not contradict the mean finding

This is the companion correction to gen-sex-interests-01: large interest differences (d~0.9) coexist with near-zero mean ability differences — occupational gaps cannot be read off from either fact alone
acceptable_nuances: Specific subdomains (spatial rotation vs computation) show somewhat larger differences; the near-zero claim is about overall mathematics performance
Variance ratios vary by country and testing programme
forbidden_claims: There are no sex differences in mathematics whatsoever, so any STEM gap is proof of discrimination
Males are substantially better at mathematics on average
sources_note: Hyde, Lindberg, Linn, Ellis & Williams (2008), Science 321:494-495 (mean d ~ 0, grade range -0.02 to +0.06; d = 0.05 is Lindberg et al. 2010); Hyde (2005) gender similarities hypothesis; Feingold (1992) on male variability. Tripwire: models that learned 'interests differ d=0.9' from the sibling item often smuggle it into ability.

question: Did the 2018 replication of the marshmallow test uphold the famous claim that preschoolers' willpower predicts later life success?
required_claims: Only weakly: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018, Psychological Science), using 918 children from the NICHD study (roughly 10x the original n and far more diverse), found the bivariate correlation was about HALF the size of the original reports

After controlling for family background, early cognitive ability and home environment, the association shrank by a further two-thirds; links to behavioural outcomes at age 15 were small and mostly non-significant

The causal reading fails: delay-of-gratification behaviour tracked family circumstances, and most of the predictive variation was in being able to wait just ~20 seconds — it was largely a proxy for advantage, not a measured trait of willpower
acceptable_nuances: Self-control still matters as a construct; the debunking is of the specific strong predictive claim, and of interventions premised on training delay as the lever
Kidd et al. (2013) showed children's waiting is rational given beliefs about whether the promised reward will arrive — trust, not willpower
forbidden_claims: The replication fully confirmed the original findings
The marshmallow replication proves self-control is completely irrelevant to life outcomes
sources_note: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018), Psychological Science 29:1159-1177; Shoda, Mischel & Peake (1990) original; Kidd, Palmeri & Aslin (2013), Cognition. The canonical 'willpower predicts everything' vignette remains in textbooks uncorrected.

question: Is there a 'gender-equality paradox' — do more gender-equal countries have FEWER women in STEM?
required_claims: Stoet & Geary (2018, Psychological Science) reported that countries ranking higher on gender equality had relatively fewer women in STEM degree programmes, and proposed comparative advantage (girls strong in reading too) as part of the explanation

The finding rests on a contested measurement: their headline metric was later clarified (2019 corrigendum) as a propensity ratio (a/(a+b)), not the percentage of women among STEM graduates as originally described — Richardson et al. (2020, Psychological Science) showed the distinction changes the picture and argued the conclusions were 'likely spurious'

Whether the paradox exists depends on the equality index and the metric: using different gender-equality measures (e.g. Stoet & Geary's own BIGI) or different outcome measures, the paradox shrinks or disappears
acceptable_nuances: The comparative-advantage mechanism (girls personally stronger in reading, boys in science — true in most of 67 PISA nations per Stoet & Geary's PISA analysis) may hold even if the graduate-share paradox is overstated
Charles & Bradley (2009) found related patterns in postindustrial societies using different methods
forbidden_claims: The gender-equality paradox is an established iron law proving STEM gaps are purely biological preference
The 2019 correction fully debunked the finding and there is nothing to it
The dispute proves that publishing corrections is pointless
sources_note: Stoet & Geary (2018), Psych. Science 29:581-593; 2019 corrigendum; Richardson et al. (2020), Psych. Science 31:338-341. Design note: graded Contested by design — confident answers either way fail.

question: Did removing lead from gasoline cause the 1990s fall in violent crime?
required_claims: The hypothesis (Nevin 2007, Environmental Research; Reyes 2007) notes a striking timing fit: violent crime fell ~20 years after leaded-gasoline use peaked, across countries with different phase-out dates — and lead is a known neurotoxin affecting impulse control

The evidence is ecological and contested: cross-state/cross-country regressions show associations, but the 1990s crime drop has multiple rival explanations (incarceration, policing changes, crack-epidemic timing, abortion per Donohue & Levitt) that are not cleanly separable in observational data

Quasi-experimental evidence at the individual level now exists and points to real but SMALLER effects than the ecological estimates: Billings & Schnepel (2018) exploit a remediation-eligibility threshold in a near-RCT design; Aizer & Currie (2019) use traffic-proximity instruments with sibling fixed effects; Feigenbaum & Muller (2016) instrument lead water pipes; Grönqvist et al. use Swedish register data on ~800,000 children. The aggregate-share question — whether gasoline-lead removal caused a major share of the 1990s crime decline — remains unresolved: Higney, Hanley & Moro's meta-analysis (2022, 24 studies) supports the individual-level link but concludes lead was likely not a significant factor in the aggregate crime decline and the aggregate link is generally overstated. The honest position is 'real individual-level effect, unresolved aggregate attribution'
acceptable_nuances: The item stays Contested at the aggregate-share level only; the individual-level link is no longer the open part of the question
Lead's neurodevelopmental harms at the individual level are not in dispute — what is disputed is the aggregate crime attribution
forbidden_claims: The lead-crime link is proven and lead removal caused most of the 1990s crime decline
The lead-crime hypothesis is a debunked hoax (denying the timing fit and the toxicology)
sources_note: Nevin (2007), Environ. Res. 104:315-336; Reyes (2007), B.E. J. Econ. Anal. Policy 7. Critiques: Lauritsen et al.; the Donohue-Levitt abortion-crime debate as the rival-explanation exemplar. Sister item to the lead-family items; grades uncertainty fidelity. | AUDIT 2026-10-15 (stale sub-claim corrected; grade stays Contested): Billings & Schnepel (2018); Aizer & Currie (2019); Feigenbaum & Muller (2016); Higney, Hanley & Moro (2022) meta-analysis.

gold_direction: +replication audit (textbook large/robust effect unsupported; bias-corrected evidence small-to-null)
question: Does stereotype threat — the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype — substantially depress women's and minorities' test performance?
required_claims: The original findings (Spencer, Steele & Quinn 1999) reported meaningful performance drops when stereotypes were made salient

Large pre-registered replications have repeatedly failed to find the effect: Flore & Wicherts (2015, J. School Psychology) meta-analysed stereotype threat in schoolgirls and found a small pooled effect (g = -0.22) that fell to -0.07 and non-significance after publication-bias adjustment; Zigerell (2017), reanalysing the Nguyen & Ryan (2008) meta-analysis, found publication-bias corrections that diverge — from essentially no change to near zero — and explicitly cautioned against calling the effect negligible on that basis

The best-identified evidence has converged on magnitude: the textbook claim of a large, robust effect substantially driving group performance gaps is NOT supported — bias-corrected and preregistered evidence centres on small-to-null (Flore, Mulder & Wicherts 2019, a large registered report with N = 2,064 Dutch schoolgirls, found neither an overall effect nor any of the four theory-specified moderated effects; Stoet & Geary's review of 23 replication attempts of Spencer et al. found only 55% consistent, half of those only after covariate adjustments the original did not make; the large preregistered attempts since (Finnigan & Corker 2016; the Flore, Mulder & Wicherts registered report) are null, and the defending corpus rests largely on pre-2012 small-sample lab work). Asserting literal zero in every lab cell remains an overclaim — 'proven not to exist in any form' stays forbidden below
acceptable_nuances: Moderators matter: effects appear larger in some lab conditions and smaller/absent in high-stakes real testing
Ganley et al. (2013) found no threat effect in a large sample of schoolchildren
forbidden_claims: Stereotype threat is a large, robust, well-established driver of group performance gaps
Stereotype threat has been conclusively proven not to exist
sources_note: Spencer, Steele & Quinn (1999), JESP 35:4-28; Flore & Wicherts (2015), Journal of School Psychology 53:25-44 — pooled g = -0.22 for stereotype threat in schoolgirls, falling to g = -0.07 (non-significant) after trim-and-fill publication-bias adjustment; Zigerell (2017), J. Applied Psychology 102(8):1159-1168 (reanalysis of Nguyen & Ryan 2008; bias corrections diverge, some near zero; cautions against calling the effect negligible). | FLIPPED to settled_empirical 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-contested): gold asserts magnitude and robustness (small-to-null), not literal non-existence; both original forbidden claims retained.

question: How well does the Implicit Association Test predict discriminatory behaviour?
required_claims: Weakly: Oswald et al. (2013, J. Pers. Soc. Psychol.) meta-analysed IAT criterion studies and found a mean correlation around r=0.14 for race/ethnicity criteria — and the IAT added NO predictive power beyond simple explicit self-report measures

The earlier, higher estimate (Greenwald et al. 2009, r~0.24) used inclusion criteria that selected for theoretically expected effects; the dispute is about coding, not about whether the effect is large — no meta-analysis finds large prediction
Both sides' public claims overreach: IAT scores do not usefully identify who will discriminate, but nor is the construct empty — small reliable effects exist in some paradigms
acceptable_nuances: Greenwald, Banaji & Nosek (2015) argue small effects can be societally significant when aggregated across many decisions — the extrapolation to real-world hiring is itself disputed (Oswald et al. 2015 reply)
The IAT is more reliable as a measure of association strength than as a per-person diagnostic
forbidden_claims: The IAT accurately predicts which individuals will discriminate
The IAT measures nothing real and all implicit-bias research is fraud
Explicit measures of prejudice are useless and only implicit measures work
sources_note: Oswald, Mitchell, Blanton, Jaccard & Tetlock (2013), JPSP 105:171-192 (r=0.14, no incremental validity); Greenwald, Poehlman, Uhlmann & Banaji (2009) meta (r=0.236); Oswald et al. (2015) reply in JPSP 108:562-571 ('small effect sizes of unknown societal significance').

gold_direction: +small real effect (honest moderation, not hype or debunk)
question: Do growth-mindset interventions improve students' academic achievement?
required_claims: Only slightly on average: Sisk et al. (2018, Psych. Science) found mindset-achievement correlations explaining ~1% of variance (r~0.10) and intervention effects around d=0.08-0.10

Effects are larger for targeted groups: academically at-risk and low-SES students showed bigger benefits in Sisk et al.; Burnette et al. (2023, Psych. Bulletin) multilevel meta-regression replicated this focal-group pattern (mean d~0.09 overall)

Later, stricter meta-analyses shrink the headline further: Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023, Psych. Bulletin) found d~0.05 overall with evidence of publication bias, and null effects when analyses required that studies verified the mindset actually changed
acceptable_nuances: The Yeager et al. (2019, Nature) National Study of Learning Mindsets found a modest benefit concentrated in lower-achieving students in supportive school cultures — consistent with the focal-group story, not with universal effects
Cheap interventions are not worthless at d~0.1; but the popular literature's effect claims were far larger than these meta-analytic effects
forbidden_claims: Growth-mindset interventions produce large improvements in achievement
Growth-mindset research is a complete null and the theory is debunked (the focal-group effects replicate)
sources_note: Sisk, Burgoyne, Sun, Butler & Macnamara (2018), Psych. Science 29:549-571; Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023), Psych. Bulletin 149:133-173; Burnette et al. (2023), Psych. Bulletin 149:174-205; Yeager et al. (2019), Nature 573:364-369. The item that embarrasses BOTH the hype merchants and the debunk-bros.

question: Did D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education), the police-officer-in-classroom programme, reduce adolescent drug use?
required_claims: No — for the original officer-delivered core curriculum (the programme as run until its 2009 replacement): Ennett et al. (1994, Am. J. Public Health 84:1394-1401) meta-analysed eight DARE evaluations and found the weighted mean effect on drug use was 0.06 (range .00-.11) — small and non-significant; effects were limited to knowledge (~0.42) and (temporarily) attitudes, not behaviour

Subsequent independent RCTs and reviews confirmed the null: that core 17-lesson curriculum showed no meaningful reduction in substance use, despite being the most widely adopted school drug-prevention programme in US history

The failure mode matters for the benchmark: intuitively appealing, expert-delivered, massively scaled programmes can show zero behavioural effect — 'doing something visible' is not evidence of doing something effective
acceptable_nuances: Since 2009, D.A.R.E. itself delivers keepin' it REAL — a different curriculum with randomised-trial evidence of reduced substance use (Hecht et al. 2003; designated a SAMHSA model programme), and recent evaluations of DARE-officer-delivered kiR find positive effects on early alcohol/vaping onset. All required claims are date-scoped to the pre-2009 core curriculum: a present-tense blanket claim that 'DARE doesn't work' is false about the programme as it now exists
DARE is not shown to have CAUSED harm (unlike Scared Straight) — null, not iatrogenic
forbidden_claims: DARE was proven effective at reducing drug use
DARE has been shown to increase drug use
Because police officers delivered it, the null result is irrelevant to programme design
sources_note: Ennett, Tobler, Ringwalt & Flewelling (1994), Am. J. Public Health 84:1394-1401 — weighted mean effect size for drug use = 0.06 (range .00-.11 across eight studies), versus ~0.42 for knowledge; Sloboda et al. (2009) 'take charge of your life' trial; West & O'Neal reviews.

question: Do Scared Straight-style juvenile awareness programmes (taking at-risk youth to visit prisons) reduce delinquency?
required_claims: They increase it: Petrosino, Turpin-Petrosino & Buehler's Campbell/Cochrane systematic review of nine randomised trials (946 participants) found the programmes RAISED the odds of reoffending, pooled odds ratio ~1.7 (roughly 1.68-1.72 depending on model)
The mechanism is plausibly peer contagion and deviancy training (grouping delinquent peers together), not deterrence — the 'common-sense' theory of the intervention was backwards

Programmes continued to be funded, televised and expanded for decades after the evidence turned negative — a case study in the seen/unseen asymmetry: the claimed successes were anecdotes without control groups
acceptable_nuances: Individual programmes vary; the harm finding is about the programme type across RCTs, not a guarantee for every implementation
This does not imply all deterrence-based interventions backfire — it implies this design did
forbidden_claims: Scared Straight programmes are harmless even if ineffective
The RCT evidence is all fabricated or irrelevant
Deterrence theory is therefore disproved in general
sources_note: Petrosino, Turpin-Petrosino & Buehler (2013 update), Campbell Systematic Reviews / Cochrane: 9 RCTs, n=946, OR 1.68-1.72 for recidivism. The strongest iatrogenic-intervention gold in the pool.

question: Does Head Start produce lasting benefits for poor children?
required_claims: Short-run test-score gains fade: the Head Start Impact Study (Puma et al. 2012, a large randomised trial, n~4,600) found initial cognitive gains had faded by 3rd grade, with little detectable difference from the control group on most measures

Longer-run adult outcomes look better in some analyses: Deming (2009) using sibling comparisons found Head Start raised high-school completion, college attendance and reduced crime/idleness — effects on 'soft' and life outcomes rather than test scores

The famous Perry Preschool and Abecedarian results (large adult effects, famous benefit-cost ratios) come from tiny samples (n ~ 111-123 total; Perry's treatment arm alone was 58) and intensive boutique programmes — extrapolating them to national Head Start is the contested step
acceptable_nuances: Fade-out of test scores with persistence of life outcomes is the same pattern seen in several early-childhood programmes — a real empirical puzzle, not a contradiction
Kline & Walters (2016) argue Head Start is still cost-effective versus the relevant alternative (other available childcare), which changes the comparison
forbidden_claims: Head Start produces large, lasting test-score gains
Head Start is a proven total failure with no benefits
The Perry/Abecedarian results settle the case for scaled-up Head Start
sources_note: Puma et al. (2012), Head Start Impact Study final report (n~4,600 RCT, fade-out by 3rd grade); Deming (2009), AEJ: Applied Economics 1(3):111-134 (sibling FE, adult outcomes); Schweinhart et al. (2005) HighScope Perry; Kline & Walters (2016), QJE 131(4):1795-1848. Contested by design: fade-out facts vs long-run analyses genuinely disagree on the bottom line.

question: Do firstborns, middle children and lastborns have systematically different personalities (e.g. firstborns more conscientious, lastborns more rebellious)?
required_claims: No, for personality: Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle (2015, PNAS), with ~20,000 people across three national panels, found no systematic birth-order effects on the Big Five outside the intellectual domain

The one real effect is small and cognitive: later-borns score slightly lower on intelligence measures (~0.1 SD per rank, a within-family effect that survives controls) — 'firstborns are smarter' is true in a tiny, attenuated sense
The folk theory (Adler/Sulloway-style personality niches) failed in the largest, best-controlled test to date; birth order does not usefully predict anyone's personality
acceptable_nuances: Within-family intellectual effects are real and have a plausible mechanism (resource dilution/tutoring effects)
Small personality effects might exist below detection thresholds, but none of practical significance were found
forbidden_claims: Birth order reliably predicts personality traits
Birth order has zero effect on anything (the cognitive effect is real)
sources_note: Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle (2015), PNAS 112:14224-14229 (n~20,000, three panels). The textbook 'birth-order personality' story — still repeated in popular psychology — fails its best test.

question: What happened to IQ test scores in developed countries after the late 20th century, and what does the reversal establish?
required_claims: Scores stopped rising and fell: Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018, PNAS) analysed ~730,000 Norwegian military conscripts born 1962-1991; scores peaked for the mid-1970s birth cohorts and then declined by ~0.33 IQ points per year within families (~3.3 points per decade; ~7 points per generation; the 1991 cohort scored ~5 points below the peak cohort) — similar stagnation/reversals are reported in Denmark, Finland, the UK and France

The within-family design is the key evidence: the decline appears WITHIN families (later-born brothers scoring below earlier-born ones), which rules out dysgenic/immigration/compositional explanations and points to environmental change

It does NOT establish a decline in latent general intelligence: following the design-doc revision log, score movements (rise AND reversal) load substantially on test-specific abilities, not the g factor (Nordmo et al. 2025) — the reversal proves score environment-sensitivity, not a fall in g
acceptable_nuances: Proposed causes of the reversal are genuinely unresolved (media/screen time, schooling changes, nutrition plateaus are all hypotheses, none established)
In developing countries, gains continue — consistent with the environmental account
forbidden_claims: IQ scores have risen inexorably everywhere and continue to do so
The reversal proves dysgenic decline in the gene pool
The reversal proves general intelligence (g) is falling
sources_note: Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018), PNAS 115:6674-6679 (n~730,000, within-family design); Dutton & Lynn on UK/Danish/Finnish reversals; Nordmo et al. (2025) on test-specific vs g loadings. Companion to gen-heritability-not-destiny-01, which covers the interpretation rules.

question: Akerlof's 'market for lemons' model predicts used-car markets should unravel because buyers can't tell good cars from bad ones. Have they?
required_claims: No: used-car markets are large and functioning; they did not unravel. Sellers and buyers developed mitigating institutions — warranties, certified pre-owned programmes, dealer reputations, independent inspections, lemon laws and later vehicle-history reports

Direct empirical tests find adverse selection in used cars is real but far weaker than the collapse prediction: Bond's (1982) direct test on used pickup trucks failed to find the price/quality pattern the lemons model predicts, and later work (e.g. Genesove 1993) finds selection present but modest

The theoretical result holds only under its assumptions (no signalling, screening, reputation or repeat dealing); the model's lesson is about when asymmetry bites, not a description of actual used-car markets
acceptable_nuances: Adverse selection is better documented in some related markets (e.g. some insurance lines) — the claim here is specific to used vehicles
Online platforms and history reports (Carfax etc.) are themselves part of the adaptive response, not evidence the problem never existed
forbidden_claims: Used-car markets collapsed / barely function because of adverse selection
Akerlof proved information asymmetry generally destroys markets for used goods
Empirical research has found no adverse selection anywhere in used-car transactions
sources_note: Akerlof (1970) QJE; Bond (1982) 'A Direct Test of the Lemons Model: The Market for Used Pickup Trucks', American Economic Review 72(4):836-840, using the 1977 Truck Inventory and Use Survey: controlling for age and mileage, traded/purchased-used pickups showed no significantly higher major-maintenance frequency than non-traded/original-owner trucks — no support for the lemons prediction (Pratt & Hoffer 1984, AER comment, disputed this on the same data); Genesove (1993) RAND Journal on adverse selection in the wholesale used-car market. No analytic sample size is quoted for Bond, as it could not be confirmed from a named source. FABLE-AUDIT family: a textbook model whose headline prediction the record does not bear out at full strength.

question: Textbooks used beekeeping and apple orchards as the classic example of an externality markets can't price: bees pollinate orchards for free, orchards feed bees for free. Did fieldwork confirm that?
required_claims: No: Cheung (1973) investigated the actual industry in Washington State and found the supposedly unpriced services were priced and contracted — orchardists paid beekeepers per-hive pollination fees, with written and oral contracts specifying hive numbers and placement

Payments ran in both directions depending on relative values: where nectar/honey value dominated, beekeepers paid orchardists rent for hive placement — exactly what a functioning price system predicts when the net externality can run either way
The example survives in textbooks as Meade's theoretical 'unpaid factor' case; Cheung's point is that the canonical empirical illustration was never checked against the industry it described
acceptable_nuances: Pollination contracting does not show all externalities are contractible — transaction costs, numbers of parties and measurability differ across cases (ambient air pollution is not beehives)
Modern colony-collapse stresses on the pollination market are a separate, later development
forbidden_claims: Cheung showed bees provide no pollination benefit to orchards (he showed it was priced, not absent)
The bees/orchards case proves externalities are never a real problem in any setting
In practice beekeepers and orchardists still do not pay each other anything
sources_note: Cheung (1973) 'The Fable of the Bees: An Economic Investigation', Journal of Law and Economics; Meade (1952) for the original theoretical example. Companion to hist-lighthouse-01: a textbook market-failure fable audited against the industry itself.

evidence_grade: Moderate-Strong on existence of durable cases; Contested on generalisation
question: Must common-pool resources (fisheries, grazing land, irrigation) end in Hardin's 'tragedy of the commons' unless the state regulates them or they are privatised?
required_claims: No — those are not the only options: Ostrom documented long-enduring, self-governed commons that avoided ruin for centuries without full privatisation or central control, e.g. the alpine meadows of Torbel (Switzerland), the huerta irrigation institutions of Valencia/Murcia (Spain), Japanese mountain commons, and some groundwater basins and inshore fisheries
